newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS - Ecu bonds lose out as EMU approaches.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - Ecu bonds lose out as EMU approaches.

text.p: Ecu bonds are faltering and look set to remain stagnant, hampered by lack of liquidity and supply, plus a host of uncertainties concerning European Monetary Union (EMU), analysts said on Monday.
While the French government is committed to a one-for-one conversion to Euro from Ecu, there is still a risk that other countries which join EMU will not adopt this policy, they said.
"Ecu bonds are in no man's land," said Kirit Shah, executive director and chief market strategist at Sanwa International in London.
"On the one hand we benefit from the French government's promise that all Ecu bonds are going to be converted into Euros, but on the other hand not everyone is committed to a one-for-one exchange."
At 1213 GMT, September Ecu bond futures were trading at 92.30, up 14 basis points from Friday's close.
The 10-year Ecu/Bund yield spread was at 55 basis points, towards the higher end of the trading band which has held the market for most of this year.

"We haven't seen much volatility in spreads," said Shah. "This year spread trading has been pretty much within a 25-60 basis point range. That in itself tells a story that the market is languishing and biding its time before its eventual demise."

He said those who were optimistic on monetary union could buy Ecu bonds for a pick-up of 50 basis points or more. "Anything above 50 basis points and we'll probably see some buying from French based investors," said Shah. "Otherwise people are better off buying the individual markets that benefit from convergence, including the high yielders," said Shah.

David Brickman, economist at Yamaichi International in London, said the Ecu bond market would continue to track the French market closely and to show a similar underperformance in the yield spread against Bunds when OATs were weak.
"The rationale behind it is that France is key to EMU and the performance of Ecu bonds is closely linked to that," he said.
Therefore the market response to the French budget on September 18 would affect Ecu bonds, analysts said.

"There are two schools of thought. One is that regardless of whether they (the French) are fudging it effectively, they are sticking to targets, which is good for EMU and therefore the bond market will rally," said Brickman.
"The other is that fundamentally what they are doing is unstable for the long-term deficit which is not good."
He said in the near term he thought the "doubters" would win the day and the OAT/Bund spread would widen which in turn would spill into Ecu bond underperformance.
On Tuesday the French Treasury, the main issuer of Ecu bonds these days, will announce details of its monthly auction of Ecu securities to be held on Thursday.
James Mitchell, economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in London, said there was no independant movement in Ecu bonds and the market was reflecting activity in other European markets.
He said the current focus was on the European budget discusions for 1997 which looked encouraging on the information available so far.
"European markets, particularly the high yielders, should perform reasonably well over the next few months. So Ecu spreads should contract a bit further against Bunds," said Mitchell.
While there was some uncertainty on the issue of conversion into the Euro and liquidity was limited, the market was attractive on current valuations, he said.
"Basically it is a bet on EMU. The currency is trading at a discount to theoretical rates and actual yeilds are a few basis points through theoretical yields. It looks a cheap market."
